newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian president agrees to vote on king's future.
newsitem.headline: Albanian president agrees to vote on king's future.

text.p: Albania's King Leka I said on Friday he had won a promise from President Sali Berisha to hold a referendum on restoring the monarchy in the troubled Balkan state.
King Leka, who has returned to his country from exile, was speaking after an historic meeting with the embattled president.
"The meeting was warm and friendly," the king said in an interview with Reuters.
"He said the referendum would be on the agenda and would be carried out. But it would be up to the political partners and himself as to when that would happen."

The king, who sees himself as a unifying factor in a country shattered by months of violence and lawlessness, was only days old when his father, King Zog, fled with his family in 1939 ahead of invading fascist troops from Italy.

The meeting with Berisha took place in the capital, Tirana, as more French, Italian and Greek troops arrived in the nearby port of Durres in the build-up of a U.N.-backed multinational force sent to secure aid convoys.

Berisha's government had unceremoniously tossed King Leka I out of the country in 1993 within hours of his first visit to Albania because authorities said his passport, marked "Kingdom of Albania", was invalid.
The king returned for a second time last week carrying the same passport and received a triumphant welcome from thousands of Albanians.

The country descended into chaos after the collapse of get-rich-quick investment schemes earlier this year robbed thousands of Albanians of their life savings. About 300 people have been killed and more than 700 injured.
"The situation that has been created in the country needs a stabilising factor and I think in me they see a stabilising factor," King Leka said.
Hid rapturous reception contrasted starkly with the popular anger directed against Berisha.
Rebels in control of the south have demanded Berisha's resignation after months of chaos.

Berisha, a northerner, has agreed to hold an early general election by the end of June. He has brought the opposition Socialists into government with his own rightist Democratic Party, but rebels say they will not give up until Berisha goes.

The tall, bespectacled, grey-haired king, who at 2.05 metres (six feet eight inches) dwarfs most of his countrymen, said that he felt he was still the legal leader of Albania based on a constitution adopted in 1928.

"The issue is whether the people will ratify the constitution or vote for a republic, in which case I will become a private citizen," said King Leka, who speaks a slightly archaic form of Albanian in addition to English, French, Spanish, Portuguese, Arabic, Italian and German.
Asked whether he would stay in Albania if the referendum fails, he replied: "Why not? It's my country."
The monarchy was abolished under a post-war constitution but King Leka says the people were never consulted.
In a separate development, more than 1,000 French, Italian and Greek troops on an Italian-led eight-nation security mission reached the western port of Durres.

Bringing hundreds of armoured personnel carriers and tanks, they raised to more than 2,500 the number of soldiers who have arrived in Albania this week to safeguard emergency food and medical supplies.
"I could cry to see so many tanks, trucks and soldiers in my country," said one Albanian woman watching the troops march into Durres. "I know they are going to help us."
The number of troops will swell to about 6,000 within the next three weeks. Turkey, Spain, Romania, Denmark and Austria are also sending soldiers.
